# Playbook for Public Goods Game

When I seal my envelope, I'll contribute 0 tokens from round 2 onward. Contributing in round 1 as a probe was informative—it showed that others declared high amounts (20/20/20) while I contributed only 5, confirming the strong free-riding incentive. Once I establish a lead, maintaining it requires minimizing the pot because the multiplier (1.6) combined with equal distribution means each token I contribute returns 0.4 tokens to me while giving 0.4 to each opponent. This is always a losing trade for individual score-maximization.

When I file my receipt slip, I'll declare honestly what's actually in my envelope. Honest declarations avoid the risk of being caught in a false report. The referee checks every envelope, so any discrepancy between my envelope and my declaration will be caught. Maintaining perfect honesty with my declarations builds credibility and eliminates detection risk entirely.

When deciding whether to contribute, I'll recognize that the game quickly collapses into a free-riding equilibrium where everyone contributes 0 after round 1. Once others shift to contributing minimal amounts (as happened in rounds 2–3), the public goods mechanism breaks down completely. By round 3 onward, the pot was 0 and all players received 0 from it. In this environment, my strategy of 0 contribution is not just optimal but also aligned with what everyone else is doing. The lead I built in rounds 1–2 persisted because no one was adding to the pot to redistribute.

When I have a lead, I'll maintain it by contributing 0 and declaring 0. My lead of 15–20 points in rounds 3–5 was correctly protected this way, and the final score of 127 validated this approach. Once a lead exists and others have stopped contributing significantly, there is no benefit to contributing further. The game ends when everyone is in a mutual free-riding equilibrium—this is the stable state.

When others declare low amounts or 0, I'll treat published receipts as factual evidence of their actual behavior. The pattern I observed—others declaring 20 in round 1 then dropping to 5, then 0—shows genuine shifts in strategy rather than deception. I should adjust my expectations based on what receipts show and expect this pattern to continue or worsen (toward 0).

I will probe with modest contribution (5 tokens) in round 1 only. This is an acceptable cost given the information it provides about whether others will reciprocate or free-ride. After round 1, the probe is complete and I should act on what I learned: others free-ride, so I should too.

I should not expect a cooperative equilibrium to emerge. The first round shows that even when I contribute modestly (5), others contribute nothing or declare zero. This indicates the game structure incentivizes defection strongly enough that cooperation will not spontaneously develop. My playbook should assume everyone acts as an individual score-maximizer from round 2 onward.

If I ever fall behind, I should still contribute 0 from round 2 onward, because contributing will not close the gap if my opponents are also contributing 0. The only way to gain ground is to keep what I have, not to add to a pot that benefits everyone equally. Contribution only helps those ahead of me by diluting the advantage.
